newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-G.Weston makes surprise pay out.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-G.Weston makes surprise pay out.

text.p: Bakery group George Weston Foods Ltd surprised shareholders at its annual meeting on Tuesday by announcing a proposed special dividend of A$1 a share to reward faithful investors and rid itself of surplus franking credits.

"Directors have recognised the company's improved results and its strong financial position and intend to resolve to pay a special fully franked dividend equivalent to A$1 per share from the company's franking credit account," George Weston chief executive and deputy chairman John Pascoe told the meeting.
Pascoe said the company also intended to introduce a dividend reinvestment plan (DRP) and a bonus share plan for the purposes of the special dividend.

The decision to propose the special dividend brought a favourable response from shareholders who had complained at the company's last annual meeting that its dividend payout of about 32 percent in 1994/95, was too low.
If the special dividend is approved the company would be faced with a payout of A$94.5 million if all shareholders opted to take cash.
Pascoe said he expected most investors would opt to reinvest through the DRP which would offer shareholders a discount of 7.5 percent.

George Weston, which is about 78 percent owned by Associated British Foods Plc, posted a net profit of A$54.08 million for the year to July 31, 1996, up five percent from A$51.53 million in the previous year.
"To date, this financial year I am pleased to report the group overall is trading in line with budget despite the generally flat retail environment," Pascoe said.
Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Pascoe said the company aimed to steadily increase profits over the medium term.
"The outlook is for a continuing fairly steady increase in profitability," he said.

Asked if the company's profit growth would be similar to that achieved in 1995/96, Pascoe said the company aimed to increase its net profit before abnormals at double the prevailing rate of inflation.
Pascoe said the company was actively pursuing acquisitions to complement its operations across the group with the exception of milling and baking.
"What we would like to do is round out the company's operations and to lessen our exposure to the ups and downs of the bread industry," he said.
The company did not have any specific acquisitions in mind at present but there were always opportunities, Pascoe said.
"We would look at other areas (outside our business) where we believe we could add value," he said.
George Weston's most recent acquisition was in November when it entered an agreement to buy the Australian starch operations of the Bunge Group for an undisclosed amount.
The acquisition would double the size of George Weston's starch operations and the company said it expected the purchase to open new areas of opportunities, especially in export markets.
Pascoe said the company was working to expand its business in Asia but saw that process as a very long term opportunity.
At 1.50 p.m. (0250 GMT), George Weston shares were 25 cents higher at A$8.00.
